Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 30, verse 9:

His Exalted and Majestic words:

﴿Have they not travelled through the earth and seen how was the end of those before them? This is also a reproach and rebuke for their having travelled and looked around, meaning that this did not benefit them, since they did not act upon the lesson and the fear of the consequence.

The judge Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

It does not apply to the disbelievers that one of them might object, saying: "I did not travel." For every person among mankind who travelled has transmitted [what he saw] to those who did not travel, so knowledge is equal, certainty is attained for all, and the proof is established. This is clear.

As for His saying, ﴿and they stirred up the earth﴾, it means: through buildings, tillage, and wars. All the buildings they constructed are of this kind of stirring up, some of it literally and some of it figuratively, because stirring up the people of the earth, the animals and the goods, is a stirring up of the earth. Abu Ja'far recited "wa-ātharū" (وَآثارُوا) with a lengthened hamza. Ibn Mujahid said: "This is nothing." Abu al-Fath said: its explanation is that he elongated the fatha of the hamza so that an alif arose, and similar to it is the verse of Ibn Harma:

"So you, from the calamities when you are struck, / and from the blame of men, are not one who is removed."

He said: "This is one of the necessities of poetry and does not occur in the Qur'an." Abu Haywa recited "wa-ātharū" (وَآثَرُوا) with a lengthened alif and without an alif after the thā', from al-athara (الأثَرَة, preference for self). The pronoun in "'amarūhā" the first time refers to those who came before, and the second time to those present and contemporary. The rest of the verse is clear, containing admonition and warning from Allah, Exalted is He.

**Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 30, verses 10–13:**

His Exalted and Majestic saying:

﴿Then the end of those who did evil was the worst, because they denied the signs of Allah and used to mock them.﴾ ﴿Allah originates creation, then repeats it, then to Him you will be returned.﴾ ﴿And on the Day the Hour is established, the criminals will be dumbfounded.﴾ ﴿And they will have no intercessors from their associates, and they will disbelieve in their associates.﴾

Ibn Kathir, Nafi' and Abu 'Amr read "ʿāqibatu" (ʿāqibah, "end/outcome") with a damma, as the subject of "kāna" (kāna, "was"). The predicate may be "al-sūʾā" (al-sūʾā, "the worst"), or it may be "an kadhdhabū" (an kadhdhabū, "that they denied"). In this case "al-sūʾā" is the object of "asāʾū" (asāʾū, "they did evil"). If "al-sūʾā" is the predicate, then "an kadhdhabū" is a causative object (mafʿūl li-ajlih, "object of purpose"), and it cannot be linked to "asāʾū", because that would separate the relative clause from its complement by the predicate of "kāna".

ʿĀṣim, Ibn ʿĀmir, Ḥamzah and al-Kisāʾī read "ʿāqibata" with a fatḥa, as the predicate placed first (khabar muqaddam), and the subject of "kāna" is one of what precedes. "Al-sūʾā" is a verbal noun (maṣdar) like "al-rujʿā", "al-futyā" and "al-shūrā". It may also be an adjective of an elided noun, whose implied sense is "the evil condition" (al-khullah al-sūʾā). Abu Hatim said: this is the reading of the common readers, with a long vowel on the waw, a fatḥa on the hamzah and the feminine ya'. Some readers emphasized it, and some inclined it.

al-Ḥasan read "al-sūʾa" with the masculine form. It is narrated from ʿUthmān ibn ʿAffān, may Allah be pleased with him, that he said: "Al-sūʾu and al-sūʾā, recite whichever you wish." Ibn ʿAbbās, may Allah be pleased with them both, said: "Asāʾū" here means "kafarū" (disbelieved), and "al-sūʾā" is the Fire. The denial of the signs of Allah, blessed and exalted, is other than mocking them; therefore He counted the two actions against them.

Then He, exalted, informed in an unrestricted manner, for all the world, about the gathering and the resurrection from the graves. Ṭalḥah and Ibn Masʿūd read "yubdiʾu" with a damma on the ya' and a kasra on the dal. The majority of readers read "turjaʿūn" with a ta' at the beginning. Abu ʿAmr and Abu Bakr from ʿĀṣim read it with a ya'.

His saying "yawma" (yawma, "on the day") is in the accusative, governed by "yublisu" (yublisu, "will be dumbfounded"). "Al-Iblās" (al-iblās, "dumbfounding") is being in an evil state together with despair of any good in that very evil; so their dumbfounding is in the punishment of Allah, exalted. The majority of readers read it with a kasra on the lam. Abu ʿAbd al-Raḥmān and the Commander of the Faithful ʿAlī ibn Abi Ṭālib, may Allah be pleased with him, read it with a fatḥa. "Ablasa al-rabʿu" means the abode became worn out, as though it despaired of being inhabited. From this is the saying of al-ʿAjjāj:

*O companion, do you know a dwelling that is effaced?*
*He said: Yes, I know it, and it has become desolate.*

The majority of readers read "wa-lam yakun lahum" with a ya' below. It is narrated from Nafi' "takun" with a ta' above. "Al-shurakāʾ" (al-shurakāʾ, "the associates"): those referred to are the idols, namely those whom they used to make partners with Allah in their claim.

His saying "wa-kānū" (wa-kānū, "and they were") means they will be, at the moment of witnessing the command of Allah, exalted, and the corruption of the state of the idols. He expressed it in the past tense for the certainty of the matter and the truth of its occurrence.

Allah the Exalted says:

"Yatafarraquun" (they will be divided) means: in their abodes, their judgments and their recompense. Qatadah said: "It is a division, by Allah, after which there is no reunion."

"Yuhbarun" (made joyful) means: they will be made to enjoy blessings. This was said by Mujahid. Al-habrah and al-hubur mean: joy and blessing. Yahya ibn Abi Kathir said: "Yuhbarun" means: they will listen to songs, and this is a kind of habrah. Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, said: "Yuhbarun" means: they will be honoured. In the proverb: "Their houses were filled with habrah, so they look at the 'ibrah (lesson)." From this is the verse of Abu Dhu'ayb:

"Separation is like the cutting of the tooth, so be patient; for indeed, for every people there is a lesson (ibrah) and joy (hubur)."

This is according to this narration. It is also narrated as "'athrah wa jubur" (a stumble and a mending), but the former is more common.

Allah mentioned the meadow (rawdah) because it is among the most beautiful places known on earth, where green vegetation abounds. What is higher in elevation is more beautiful. From this is the saying of al-A'sha:

"No meadow of the meadows of al-Hazn, luxuriant, green, upon which a pouring, abundant rain has fallen."

From this is also the saying of Kuthayyir:

"No meadow in al-Hazn is sweet of soil, whose dew is poured forth by its jathjath and its 'arar (plants)."

Al-Asma'i said: "Rawdah is not said unless there is water in it from which one can drink."

Allah's saying "So glorify Allah" is an address to the believers, commanding worship and urging prayer at these times, as if He says: this division has led to kinds of blessings and punishment, and the believer proceeds on the path of success through the mercy of Allah. Ibn 'Abbas, Qatadah and some jurists said: in this verse there is an indication of four prayers: Maghrib, Subh, 'Asr and Zuhr. They said: and 'Isha' is in another verse, in "zulafan min al-layl" (at the approaches of the night), and in the mention of the times of 'awrah (nakedness). Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, also said, and a group of jurists said: in this verse there is an indication of the five prayers, because His saying "when you enter the evening" includes two prayers.

Allah's saying "And to Him belongs all praise in the heavens and the earth" is an interjection between the two statements, of the type that exalts Allah the Exalted and urges worship of Him. Ikrimah recited: "hina tumsuna wa hinan tusbihuna" (with the second word read as hinan, "at a time"), and the meaning is: "when you enter the evening in it, and at a time when you enter the morning in it."

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 30, verses 19–22:

His, the Mighty and Majestic, saying:

﴿He brings forth the living from the dead, and brings forth the dead from the living, and gives life to the earth after its death. And thus shall you be brought forth.﴾ ﴿And among His signs is that He created you from dust; then, behold, you are human beings spreading abroad.﴾ ﴿And among His signs is that He created for you spouses from among yourselves, that you may find tranquility in them; and He placed between you affection and mercy. Indeed in that are signs for a people who reflect.﴾ ﴿And among His signs is the creation of the heavens and the earth, and the diversity of your tongues and your colours. Indeed in that are signs for those who have knowledge.﴾

"Al-hayy" (the living) and "al-mayyit" (the dead) in this verse are used both literally and figuratively. The literal sense: the semen from which a human emerges, and the egg from which a bird emerges, which is itself dead, emerging from a living thing, and what follows this pattern. In this sense Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them, interpreted it. Al-Hasan said the meaning is: the believer from the unbeliever, and the unbeliever from the believer.

The qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said: This meaning has also been related from the Prophet ﷺ that he recited this verse when Umm Kulthum bint 'Uqba bin Abi Mu'ayt spoke to him about Islam. The figurative sense is the bringing forth of green plants from the earth, and the bringing forth of food from plants, and what follows this pattern. He gave as an example the revival of the earth after its death by rain.

Then, after these examples which rationally establish the possibility of the resurrection of bodies, He stated the report that likewise we shall be brought forth from the graves. A group read "yukhrajun" with the yā' from beneath; the general readers read "tukhrajun" with a damma on the tā'. Al-Hasan, Ibn Wabbab, al-A'mash and Talha read it with a fatha on the tā' and a damma on the rā'.

He said, "created you" in the sense that He created your father Adam; this was said by Qatada. "Tantashirun" means: you move about freely and disperse in the lands and on journeys.

As for His saying, the Exalted: ﴿from among yourselves﴾, it may mean His creating Hawwa' from the rib of Adam, and this is applied to all women, since their mother was created from the very self of Adam, i.e., from his own person. It may also mean: from your own kind and your own species. "Mawadda" and "rahma" are taken in their well-known meanings of mutual love and compassion; this is the eloquent reading. Mujahid, al-Hasan and 'Ikrima said: by "mawadda" is meant intercourse and by "rahma" is meant offspring.

Then the Exalted drew attention to the creation of the heavens and the earth, and the difference of languages and colours, and these are whiteness, blackness and others. It may also mean the varieties and kinds of the children of Adam, so that it encompasses the persons of mankind who differ in colours, and it encompasses the tongues. The majority of readers read "lil-'alamin" with a fatha on the lam; Hafs from 'Asim read "lil-'alimin" with a kasra on the lam. The former means that this verse itself is directed to the whole world, while the latter means that those who benefit from reflecting upon it are only the people of knowledge.

﴿He brings forth the living from the dead, and brings forth the dead from the living, and gives life to the earth after its death. And thus shall you be brought forth.﴾ ﴿And among His signs is that He created you from dust; then, behold, you are human beings spreading abroad.﴾ ﴿And among His signs is that He created for you spouses from among yourselves, that you may find tranquility in them; and He placed between you affection and mercy. Indeed in that are signs for a people who reflect.﴾ ﴿And among His signs is the creation of the heavens and the earth, and the diversity of your tongues and your colours. Indeed in that are signs for those who have knowledge.﴾

"Al-hayy" (the living) and "al-mayyit" (the dead) in this verse are used both literally and figuratively. The literal sense: the semen from which a human emerges, and the egg from which a bird emerges, which is itself dead, emerging from a living thing, and what follows this pattern. In this sense Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them, interpreted it. Al-Hasan said the meaning is: the believer from the unbeliever, and the unbeliever from the believer.

The qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said: This meaning has also been related from the Prophet ﷺ that he recited this verse when Umm Kulthum bint 'Uqba bin Abi Mu'ayt spoke to him about Islam. The figurative sense is the bringing forth of green plants from the earth, and the bringing forth of food from plants, and what follows this pattern. He gave as an example the revival of the earth after its death by rain.

Then, after these examples which rationally establish the possibility of the resurrection of bodies, He stated the report that likewise we shall be brought forth from the graves. A group read "yukhrajun" with the yā' from beneath; the general readers read "tukhrajun" with a damma on the tā'. Al-Hasan, Ibn Wabbab, al-A'mash and Talha read it with a fatha on the tā' and a damma on the rā'.

The "min" in His saying, blessed and exalted is He, ﴿And among His signs is that He created you﴾ is partitive (lil-tab'id). He said, "created you" in the sense that He created your father Adam; this was said by Qatada. "Tantashirun" means: you move about freely and disperse in the lands and on journeys.

As for His saying, the Exalted: ﴿from among yourselves﴾, it may mean His creating Hawwa' from the rib of Adam, and this is applied to all women, since their mother was created from the very self of Adam, i.e., from his own person. It may also mean: from your own kind and your own species. "Mawadda" and "rahma" are taken in their well-known meanings of mutual love and compassion; this is the eloquent reading. Mujahid, al-Hasan and 'Ikrima said: by "mawadda" is meant intercourse and by "rahma" is meant offspring.

Then the Exalted drew attention to the creation of the heavens and the earth, and the difference of languages and colours, and these are whiteness, blackness and others. It may also mean the varieties and kinds of the children of Adam, so that it encompasses the persons of mankind who differ in colours, and it encompasses the tongues. The majority of readers read "lil-'alamin" with a fatha on the lam; Hafs from 'Asim read "lil-'alimin" with a kasra on the lam. The former means that this verse itself is directed to the whole world, while the latter means that those who benefit from reflecting upon it are only the people of knowledge.

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 30, verses 23–25:

His, the Exalted and Majestic, saying:

﴿And among His signs is your sleep by night and by day, and your seeking of His bounty. Surely in that are signs for a people who hear.﴾ ﴿And among His signs He shows you the lightning, in fear and in hope, and He sends down water from the sky, and by it gives life to the earth after its death. Surely in that are signs for a people who reason.﴾ ﴿And among His signs is that the heaven and the earth stand by His command. Then when He calls you with a single call from the earth, behold, you will come forth.﴾

He, exalted, mentioned sleep "by night and by day," but the common usage (al-'urf) of sleeping is only at night. Then He mentioned seeking His bounty as though it were in both. The meaning of that is that it encompasses night and day, so He named the time (al-zaman) and intended by it the enumeration of the sign of sleep and the enumeration of the sign of seeking bounty. For these are two signs and two blessings, which occur in a night and a day. The common usage is that each of the two blessings is "confined" (tahayyuz), i.e., its place is mostly in one of them. Some exegetes (mufassirun) said: there is a transposition (taqdim wa ta'khir) in the speech.

(p-18) The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

This is weak. He only intended to arrange sleep for the night and seeking for the day, and the wording of the verse does not give what he intended.

As for His saying, ﴿yurikum﴾ (He shows you), it is a verb in the nominative case (marfu'), because the particle "an" (that) was omitted, which, had it been present, would have put it in the accusative. When the verb took the place of a noun, it was given the nominative inflection (i'rab). Its parallel is the saying of Tarafah:

Unquestionably, O you who rebuke me, (for) attending the battle and that I witness pleasures, will you make me immortal?

Al-Rummani said: The verse may allow that the sense is: "And among His signs is a sign: He shows you the lightning," and the word "sign" (ayah) was omitted because the particle "min" (among) indicates it. From this is the saying of the poet:

Time is nothing but two turns, so from them: one I die, and another I seek life, striving.

The sense is: from them, a turn in which I die.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

This is according to the view that "min" is partitive (lil-tab'id), like the rest of these signs. It is possible that in this verse alone "min" is for the beginning of the extent (li-ibtida' al-ghayah), so there is no need to estimate "ayah," and the verb is then purely for the future tense.

(p-19) As for His saying, ﴿fear and hope﴾, Qatadah said: fear for the traveller and hope for the one who stays home.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

There is no basis for this specification or similar ones; rather, fear and hope are present for every human being. Al-Dahhak said: The fear is of His thunderbolts, and the hope is for His rain.

As for His saying, ﴿that the heaven and the earth stand﴾, its meaning is: they remain firm, as in His saying, ﴿And when the night darkens over them, they stand still﴾ [al-Baqarah: 20]. This is common. It was also said: it is a verb in the future form, placed in the position of the past, so as to give it the sense of continuity (dawam) which belongs to the future. "The call from the earth" is the resurrection on the Day of Resurrection. "From the earth" is a circumstantial phrase (hal) for those addressed, as if He said: coming out of the earth. It is also permissible that "from the earth" is a qualifier (sifah) of the call.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

In my view, "min" here is for the end of the extent (li-intiha' al-ghayah), as you say: "Your call is from the mountain," when the one called is on the mountain. The pause (waqf) in this verse according to Nafi' and Ya'qub al-Hadrami is on "da'wah" (a call), and the meaning is: after, when you come out from the earth. This is on the view that "min" is for the beginning of the extent. Makki said: The better view according to the people of reflection (ahl al-nazar) is that the pause is at the end of the verse, because the view of Sibawayh and al-Khalil regarding the second "idha" is that it is the response (jawab) of the first, as if He said: then when He calls you, you come out. This is the most solid of the views. Hamzah and al-Kisa'i read ﴿takhrujun﴾ with a fatha on the ta', and the rest read ﴿tukhrajun﴾ with a damma on the ta'.

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 30, verse 26–28:

The words of the Mighty and Majestic:

﴿To Him belongs whoever is in the heavens and the earth. All are devoutly obedient to Him.﴾ ﴿It is He who originates creation and then repeats it, and that is easier for Him. To Him belongs the highest likeness in the heavens and the earth, and He is the Mighty, the Wise.﴾ ﴿He presents to you a parable from yourselves: Do you have among those whom your right hands possess any partners in what We have provided for you, so that you are equal therein and you fear them as you fear one another among yourselves? Thus do We detail the signs for a people who reason.﴾

The lam in the first lahu is the lam of possession (lam al-milk). In the second, it is the lam of transitivity for qanata (to be devoutly obedient). Qanata means to submit (khada'a) in obedience and compliance. The apparent wording of this verse is general, both regarding those who are devoutly obedient and regarding everyone who has intellect. Generalizing this in meaning is not sound, because it is a statement of fact, and we find that many of the jinn and humankind are not devoutly obedient in many beliefs and actions. Therefore the general apparent meaning of this verse must mean a particular sense. The interpreters differed over where this particularity lies.

Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him, said: it lies in devout obedience and submission. This is because everyone who has intellect is devoutly obedient to Allah in most matters of life and death, provision, power and the like, while some of them withhold worship and beliefs and so are not devoutly obedient in them. It is as if He said: All are devoutly obedient to Him in most matters and in the greater part of affairs.

Ibn Zayd said, in substance: the particularity lies in the individuals mentioned, as if He said: To Him belongs whoever is in the heavens and the earth, of angels and believers.

His words ﴿originates creation﴾ mean: He brings it into being and produces it from non-existence. The verb came in the present form because this meaning applies to what has already passed, such as Adam and the generations before, and to what will come in the future; the present form encompasses all of this. "Repeats it" means He resurrects it from the graves and brings it into being another time.

The interpreters differed over His words, exalted is He, ﴿and that is easier for Him﴾. Ibn 'Abbas and Rabi' ibn Khaytham said: the meaning is "and it is easy for Him" (hayyin). A parallel to this is the words of the poet:

; By your life, I do not know, and indeed I am fearful (la-awjal)

meaning lawajil (fearful). And the words of another:

; a house whose pillars are mightier and taller

And their saying in the adhan: "Allahu akbar", and the words of al-Shafi'i, may Allah have mercy on him:

; That is a path in which I am not the only one (bi-awhad)

meaning "bi-wahid" (not unique). Abu 'Ubayda cited this verse as evidence, and this is abundant evidence. In some copies of the Qur'an it reads: "wa-kullun hayyinun 'alayhi" (and all of it is easy for Him).

Ibn 'Abbas also said, as did Mujahid and 'Ikrima: the meaning is "and that is easier for Him" (aysar 'alayhi), even though everything is equally easy for Him in one state and one condition. He said: but this preference is according to human belief and what observation of the visible world gives them, that repetition of many things is easier for us than initiation, since it requires less practice and does not need the deliberation that initiation needed. These two views have their pronouns referring to Allah, blessed and exalted is He.

Another group said: the pronoun in "alayhi" refers to "creation" (al-khalq).

The qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

Then it means "the created being" only. According to the first two interpretations, it may mean "the created being" or be a verbal noun from "khalaqa". Al-Hasan said: repetition is easier for the created being than its initiation, because in its initiation it passes from state to state, from a drop of semen to a clinging clot to a lump of flesh and the like, whereas in repetition it occurs in a single moment. It is as if He said: "and it is easier for Him", i.e., shorter in duration and less in transition.

Some of them said: "and it is easier for the created being to repeat a thing after bringing it into being; this is the custom of created beings, so how do you deny repetition in the case of the Creator?"

The qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

The more apparent view to me is that the pronoun refers to Allah, exalted is He. This is supported by His words ﴿To Him belongs the highest likeness﴾, since what came in wording that involves metaphor and drawing a comparison from created beings to the Creator, and likening Him to what people know from themselves, purified the aspect of greatness by making for Him the highest likeness, which no modality reaches and no resemblance to anything attains. "The Mighty" and "the Wise" are two attributes that agree with the meaning of the verse, for by them He repeats and His command takes effect among His servants however He wills.

Then He, exalted is He, made clear the matter of the idols and the corruption of the belief of those who associate them with Allah, by setting forth this parable. Its meaning is: O people, if you have slaves whom you own, you do not make them partners with you in your wealth, nor in your affairs, nor in anything on the basis of equal standing, and it is not part of your conduct to fear them (p-٢٣) that they will inherit your wealth or share it with you during your lifetimes, as some of you do to others. If this is so among you, how do you say that among His slaves and His possessions there are partners in His authority and divinity, and attribute to Him what does not befit you in your own estimation? This is the tafsir of Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him, and a group; and this meaning came in the form of a question and affirmation.

The readers recited ﴿kha-ifatikum anfusakum﴾ with fatha on the sin, and Ibn Abi 'Abla read it with damma. The majority read "nufassilu" with the nun, taking it as an echo of "razaqnakum", and 'Abbas, from Abu 'Amr, read "yufassilu" with the ya', taking it as an echo of "daraba lakum mathalan".

The Almighty said:

Rather, they followed their desires out of ignorance, appetite, and aiming at the affairs of their worldly life. Then, as a rebuke to them, He asked: "Who can guide when Allah has led astray?" That is, there is no guide for people in this state. Then He informed that they have no helper.

Then the Exalted commanded His Prophet (ﷺ) to set his face toward the upright religion, which is the religion of Islam. "Setting the face" means directing the aim and exerting determined effort in the acts of religion. The face is mentioned because it gathers the human senses and is the noblest of them. "Ḥanīfan" (ḥanīf) means upright, inclining away from all the distorted and abrogated (mansūkh) religions. Abrogation (naskh) here means the cancellation of a ruling by a later revelation. His saying, "the fitrah of Allah upon which He created mankind," is in the accusative as a verbal noun, like His saying: "the dye of Allah" (Q. 2:138). It was said that it is in the accusative by a hidden verb, its estimated meaning being: follow and adhere to the fitrah of Allah, the Exalted.

People differed about the meaning of fitrah here. Makkī and others mentioned all the meanings to which this word could be applied, and some of these are strained. The thing relied upon in explaining this word is that it is the natural disposition and form present in the child's very nature, which is prepared and made ready so that by it he can distinguish the creatures of Allah, the Exalted, find evidence in them for his Lord, the Majestic and Exalted, know His laws, and believe in Him. It is as if the Exalted said: set your face toward the religion which is the ḥanīf, and which is the fitrah of Allah, upon which He created mankind in readiness for it, but accidents befall them. From this is the saying of the Prophet (ﷺ): "Every child is born upon the fitrah; then his parents make him a Jew or a Christian..." (the hadith). The mention of the two parents is only an example of the accidents, which are many.

One is that by it He means this aforementioned fitrah, i.e., know that this fitrah has no alteration from the side of the Creator, and no matter comes contrary to it in any way. This meaning is: there is no alteration of the beliefs that are in the ḥanīf religion, for every sharia is its beliefs.

He interpreted His saying, blessed and exalted, "He created mankind," as specific, meaning the believers. It was said that the fitrah is the covenant which Allah, the Exalted, took from the offspring of Adam when He brought them forth as particles from his loins. Similar is the hadith of Mu'ādh, may Allah be pleased with him, when 'Umar ibn al-Khaṭṭāb, may Allah be pleased with him, passed by him and said: "O Mu'ādh, what is the foundation (qiwām) of this community?" "Al-qayyim" is an intensive form derived from "qiyām," which carries the meaning of uprightness.

The Qāḍī Abū Muḥammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

According to this, the word "association" (ishrāk) carries a figurative sense, since they became sects in their religion. "Shiya'" means sects; its singular is "shī'a." His saying, "each faction rejoicing in what it has," means that they are captivated by their opinions and pleased with their misguidance, and this is an established trait in them. A group read "farraqū dīnahum" (they separated their religion) with an alif, i.e., "fāraqū" (they parted from their religion).

Mujāhid said: the meaning is "There is no alteration of the religion of Allah," and this is the saying of Ibn Jubayr, al-Ḍaḥḥāk, Ibn Zayd, and al-Nakha'ī.

The Qāḍī Abū Muḥammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

This meaning is: there is no alteration of the beliefs that are in the ḥanīf religion, for every sharia is its beliefs.

Some exegetes went to other interpretations of this verse. Among them is the saying of Ikrima, which was narrated from Ibn 'Abbās, may Allah be pleased with them both: "There is no alteration in the creation of Allah" means the prohibition of castrating male animals. Among them is the saying of some people about fitrah: that it is the religious community (milla). It was also said that fitrah means religion. He interpreted His saying, blessed and exalted, "He created mankind," as specific, meaning the believers. It was said that the fitrah is the covenant which Allah, the Exalted, took from the offspring of Adam when He brought them forth as particles from his loins. He said: "Sincerity, which is the fitrah upon which Allah created mankind; the prayer, which is the religion; and obedience, which is protection." 'Umar, may Allah be pleased with him, said: "You have spoken the truth."

"Al-qayyim" is an intensive form derived from "qiyām," which carries the meaning of uprightness.

His saying, the Exalted, "turning in repentance" (munībīna), may be a circumstantial clause (ḥāl) of His saying "He created mankind," especially according to the view of one who holds that this refers specifically to believers. It may also be a circumstantial clause of His saying "So set your face," and it is in the plural because the address of setting the face is to the Prophet (ﷺ) and to his community. Its parallel is His saying, blessed and exalted: "O Prophet, when you divorce women" (Q. 65:1). "Munīb" means one who returns, sincere, inclining toward what his soul desires. The "polytheists" referred to in this verse are the Jews and the Christians, as said by Qatāda. Ibn Zayd said they are the Jews. 'Ā'isha and Abū Hurayra, may Allah be pleased with them both, said it refers to the people of the qibla (Muslims).

The Qāḍī Abū Muḥammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

According to this, the word "association" (ishrāk) carries a figurative sense, since they became sects in their religion. "Shiya'" means sects; its singular is "shī'a." His saying, "each faction rejoicing in what it has," means that they are captivated by their opinions and pleased with their misguidance, and this is an established trait in them. A group read "farraqū dīnahum" (they separated their religion) with an alif, i.e., "fāraqū" (they parted from their religion).

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 30, verses 33–35:

(p-26) His statement, mighty and majestic is He:

﴿When harm touches people, they call upon their Lord, turning to Him in repentance. Then when He lets them taste mercy from Him, behold, a group of them associate others with their Lord.﴾ ﴿So that they may deny what We have given them. Enjoy, then; you will soon know.﴾ ﴿Have We sent down to them any authority, so that it speaks of what they have been associating with Him?﴾

This is the beginning of a rebuke directed at the idol-worshippers who associate with God, may He be exalted, others besides Him. God, may He be exalted, explains to them that they are like the rest of mankind in that, when harm touches them, they call upon God, glorified is He, and abandon the idols, leaving them cast aside. At that time they are turning in repentance and submission. Then when He lets them taste His mercy, that is, when His command reaches them with it (the word "taste" is used metaphorically), behold, a group of them associates with Him idols and the like. The "idha" (then when) here is for suddenness (idha al-mufaja'ah), and therefore it is suitable to stand in the response to the first "idha" in the position of the fa' (so/then). This group is the idol-worshippers.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may God have mercy on him, said:

Something of these expressions also applies to the believers when relief comes to them after hardship: they attribute that to a created being, or to the cleverness of their own opinions, and the like. This is because in it there is a lack of gratitude to God, blessed and exalted, and it is called "association" (tashrik) metaphorically.

As for His statement, exalted is He: ﴿"li-yakfuru"﴾ (so that they may deny), the lam is the lam of purpose (lam kay). A group has said: it is the lam of command (lam al-amr) in the manner of threat and warning. As for His statement, exalted is He: ﴿"fa-tamatta'u"﴾ (so enjoy), it is a command in the manner of warning and rebuke, meaning: say to them, O Muhammad: "Enjoy."

Abu al-'Aliyah read "fa-yatamatta'u" with a ya' before the ta', and that is a conjunction with "li-yakfuru," meaning: so that their lifespans may be prolonged in disbelief. In the codex of Ibn Mas'ud (Ibn Mas'ud's reading) it is "fa-l-yatamatta'u" (let them enjoy). It is narrated from Abu al-'Aliyah: "fa-yumatti'u" with a damma on the ya' without the first ta'. In the Mushaf of Ibn Mas'ud it is "tamatta'u," so Harun said. The common people read "ta'lamuna" with a ta' as direct address, and Abu al-'Aliyah read "ya'lamuna" with a ya' as reference to the absent.

As for His statement, exalted is He: "am" is in the sense of "bal" (rather) together with the interrogative alif, as if He had turned away from the opening of the speech and returned to this argument. And "al-sultan" here means proof, whether from a messenger, a book, or the like. In the speech of the Arabs, "al-sultan" is the plural of "salit," like raghif and rughfan, and ghadir and ghudran. It is derived from domination (tasallut) and overpowering (taghallub), and this term has become attached among the Arabs to the chief, because he dominates by the right way. It is a collective noun in terms of the kinds of victory and sovereignty it has. Others have said it is a singular noun with the pattern fu'lan.

As for His statement, exalted is He: ﴿"fa-huwa yatakallamu"﴾ (so it speaks), its meaning is that it would reveal their argument, make their doctrine prevail, and speak of their association. This was said by Qatadah, and that takes the place of speech, as He, exalted is He, said: ﴿This Our Book speaks against you with truth﴾ [al-Jathiyah: 29].

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 30, verse 36–38:

His, the Mighty and Majestic, saying:

﴿And when We let people taste mercy, they rejoice in it; but if an evil afflicts them for what their hands have sent forth, behold, they despair.﴾ ﴿Have they not seen that Allah extends provision for whom He wills and restricts [it]? Indeed in that are signs for a people who believe.﴾ ﴿So give the relative his right, and the needy, and the wayfarer. That is better for those who desire the Face of Allah, and those are the successful.﴾

When He, exalted is He, mentioned the state of people when hardship and harm come upon them and they are delivered from it into ease, He mentioned in this verse the matter from the other side, by mentioning mercy followed by hardship. So for them, at the first level, there is supplication (taḍarru') then association (shirk), and for them, at the second, there is exultation (faraḥ) and insolence (baṭar) then despair (qunūṭ) and hopelessness (ya's). Every person takes from this disposition a share: among them are the one who has little and the one who has much, except the one upon whose heart the Sharia has fastened and who has been disciplined by the discipline of Allah, the Exalted. He is patient in adversity, thankful in ease, does not become insolent at a blessing, and does not despair at a trial.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿for what their hands have sent forth﴾, meaning: Allah tests nations, and afflicts some of them when sins become widespread and evil deeds appear. Likewise, a person may be afflicted by something on account of his own bad deeds alone, and Allah pardons much.

Al-qunūṭ: despair. Abū 'Amr and a group read "yaqniṭūn" with a kasra on the nūn, and Nāfi', al-Ḥasan, and a group read it with a fatḥa.

The answer to the conditional in His saying "in tuṣibhum" (if an evil afflicts them) is His saying "idhā hum" (behold, they), because it is the particle of sudden surprise (al-mufājaʾa), which is not used to begin a sentence, since it stands in the position of the fāʾ (of consequence), and the conditional is answered by it. As for those which are conditional, or which carry the meaning of a condition, they are used to begin a sentence.

Then He, exalted is He, mentioned the matter which, whoever considers it, does not despair of the mercy of Allah, the Exalted, in any state, namely that Allah, blessed and exalted, specifies whom He wills of His servants with the expansion of provision. So it is fitting for every servant to be hopeful of what is with his Lord. Then Allah, exalted is He, commanded His Prophet with a command in which the community is included, and this is by way of recommendation (nadb) to giving the relative his right, from the giving of wealth, good companionship, and gentle speech.

Al-Ḥasan said: "His right is consolation (mu'āsāh) in ease." He said: "Most of what is intended is the command of assistance with wealth, and from it is the saying of the Prophet ﷺ: 'In wealth there is a right besides zakat.'" And that is a right for the needy and the wayfarer. It has been explained that the right of these two is in wealth and otherwise. Likewise, it is incumbent upon a relative who is in need, whose right is fulfilled, that he also fulfill the right of his relative in goodness of companionship.

"The Face of Allah" here means the direction of His worship and His pleasure. "Al-Muflihūn": those who attain their aim, who reach their hopes.

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 30, verse 39–41:

His, the Mighty and Majestic, saying:

﴿And whatever you give in riba (usury) so that it may increase within the wealth of people, it does not increase with Allah. And whatever you give in zakah, seeking the Face of Allah, those are the ones who will receive manifold increase.﴾ ﴿It is Allah who created you, then provided for you, then will cause you to die, then will give you life. Is there any of your partners who does anything of that? Glorified is He and exalted above what they associate with Him.﴾ ﴿Corruption has appeared on land and sea by what the hands of people have earned, that He may let them taste part of what they have done, so that they may return.﴾

The majority of readers recited ﴿"wa-mā ātaytum"﴾ meaning "what you gave" (aʿtaytum). Ibn Kathir recited "wa-mā ataytum" without the long vowel, meaning "what you did," as you say: "ataytu ṣawāban" (I did what was right) and "ataytu khaṭaʾan" (I did what was wrong). They agreed on the long vowel in His saying ﴿"wa-mā ātaytum min ribā"﴾. Ribā means increase.

The interpreters differed on the meaning of this verse. Ibn ʿAbbas, Ibn Jubayr, Mujahid and Tawus said: this verse was revealed concerning gifts given for return (hibat al-thawab).

The Qadi Abu Muhammad (may Allah have mercy on him) said:

What is similar to this, of what a person does in order to be repaid for it, such as greeting and other things, is not sinful, but there is no reward in it and no increase with Allah, blessed and exalted.

Ibn ʿAbbas also said, as did Ibrahim al-Nakhaʿi: it was revealed concerning people who give to their relatives and brothers, meaning to enrich them and benefit them and show favour to them, and so that they increase their wealth by way of benefit to themselves. Al-Shaʿbi said: the meaning of the verse is that whatever a person spends on someone to serve him, and makes light of it so that he benefits in his worldly life, then that benefit, for which the service is repaid, does not increase with Allah, exalted is He.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad (may Allah have mercy on him) said:

All of this is close to being a part of the interpretation. It is also possible that the meaning of this verse is the prohibition of riba in trade. When Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, urged the benefiting of the near of kin, the needy and the traveller, He made known that what a person does of riba in order to increase his wealth thereby, and his doing of that is only within the wealth of people, then that does not increase (yarbū) or grow with Allah, exalted is He. Rather, sin and the removal of blessing attach to it. Whatever a person gives in zakah for the increase and purification of his wealth, seeking the Face of Allah, exalted is He, that is what is repaid manifold, as much as Allah wills for him.

Al-Suddi said: this verse was revealed concerning the riba of Thaqif, because they used to practise riba, and Quraysh practised it among them.

The majority of the seven readers recited ﴿"li-yarbū"﴾ with yāʾ, attributing the verb to riba. Nafiʿ alone recited "li-tarbū" with a ḍammah on the tāʾ and the wāw silent, meaning "that you may be people of increases." This is the reading of Ibn ʿAbbas (may Allah be pleased with them both), the people of Madinah, al-Hasan, Qatadah, Abu Rajaʾ and al-Shaʿbi. Abu Hatim said: it is our reading. **Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 30, verses 42–44:**

His saying, may He be exalted and glorified:

﴿Say, "Travel through the earth and observe how was the end of those before you. Most of them were polytheists."﴾ ﴿So direct your face toward the upright religion before there comes a Day from Allah which no one can avert. That Day they will be separated.﴾ ﴿Whoever disbelieves, his disbelief is upon him; and whoever does righteousness – they are preparing for themselves.﴾

This is a warning to Quraysh and a command to them to take heed regarding those nations that passed before them, and regarding the evil outcomes they met because of their disbelief and their associating partners with Allah. Then Allah, may He be exalted, commanded His Prophet, upon him be blessings and peace, to direct his face (to the religion). The meaning is: make your intention and your striving directed to the religion, that is, to its path, its deeds, and its beliefs. The word "al-Qayyim" (the upright) originally was "Qayyum." The letter *ya'* and the letter *waw* came together, and the *ya'* preceded while being *sakin* (vowelless), so the *waw* was changed into a *ya'* (*ibdal*, substitution) and the first of the two was assimilated into the second (*idgham*, assimilation). Then He, blessed and exalted, warned them of the Day of Resurrection with a warning that encompasses the whole world, and they are the intended ones (of this address). (p-٣٢) The phrase "لا مَرَدَّ لَهُ" (*la maradda lah*, "which no one can avert") means: there is no returning in it to action or to desire, nor is there any departing from it. It may also be understood to mean: no one can repel it so that it does not occur, and this is apparent according to the wording. The word "يَصَّدَّعُونَ" (*yasadda'una*, "they will be separated") means: they will scatter after having been gathered, and this is the *tasaddu'* (splitting apart). The meaning of "يَتَفَرَّقُونَ" (they scatter) is: to Paradise and to the Fire.

Then He divided the two groups by the rulings that befall them from their deeds in this world. Then He expressed disbelief by "عَلَيْهِ" (*'alayhi*, "upon him"), which conveys weight and hardship, and He expressed righteous deeds by the *lam* which is the *lam* of ownership (*lam al-milk*), "لِأنْفُسِهِمْ" (*li-anfusihim*, "for themselves"). The word "يَمْهَدُونَ" (*yamhadun*, "they are preparing") means they make ready and prepare (a place), and it is a metaphor (*isti'ara*) transferred from carpets and the like to states and ranks. Mujahid said: this preparing refers to the grave.

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 30, verse 48–50:

His, the Exalted and Majestic, saying:

﴿It is Allah who sends the winds, so they stir up clouds, and He spreads them across the sky however He wills, and makes them into fragments, so you see the rain emerging from within them. Then when He causes it to fall upon whomever of His servants He wills, behold, they rejoice﴾ ﴿And although they were, before it was sent down upon them, truly despairing﴾ ﴿So look at the traces of Allah's mercy, how He gives life to the earth after its death. Indeed, that is the One who gives life to the dead, and He is over all things Powerful﴾

Ithārat al-suḥub (the stirring of the clouds): setting them in motion from their stillness and driving them along. Their spreading in the sky is scattering them across the horizons. Al-kisaf (the fragments): pieces.

The majority of reciters read "kisafan" with a fatha on the sin. Ibn 'Amir read "kisfan" with a sukun on the sin, and this is the reading of al-Hasan, Abu Ja'far and al-A'raj. Both are forms of the plural, as it is said "sidratun wa sidrun" (with a sukun on the dal) and "sidarun" (with a fatha on the dal). Makki said: whoever reads with a sukun on the sin, its meaning is that He makes the cloud one single piece.

Al-wadq (the rain): water that falls as rain, and from it is the saying of the poet:

"Neither a rain-cloud has poured its pouring, nor a land has brought forth its herbage (ibqal)."

Khilaluhu (its gaps): the openings that lie between its parts, because it is made of loosely joined parts. The majority read "min khilalihi" with a kasra on the kha and an alif after the lam, as the plural of khalal, like jabal and jibal. ʿAli ibn Abi Talib, may Allah be pleased with him, Ibn ʿAbbas, al-Dahhak and al-Hasan (in a variant from him) read "min khilalihi" as "min khilalihi" with a fatha on the lam, which is a noun of genus. The pronoun in "khilalihi" may refer back to "al-sahab" (the clouds), or it may refer back to "al-kisaf" in the reading of whoever reads with a sukun on the sin. He made the pronoun masculine in consideration of the wording, not the meaning of plurality, just as you say "hadha tamarun jayyid" and "min al-shajari al-akhdari naran". Whoever reads "kisafan" with a fatha on the sin refers the pronoun only to the clouds.

His, the Exalted and Majestic, saying: "min qablihi" is an emphatic addition, which conveys the information of how swiftly human hearts turn from despair to rejoicing. This is because His saying "min qabli an yunazzala ʿalayhim" may allow for a span of time, meaning: before that, i.e., before it descends after many days or the like. So His saying "min qablihi" carries the sense that this is connected to the rain, so it is a useful emphasis. Yaʿqub, ʿIsa and Abu ʿAmr (in a variant from him) read "yunzilu" with a light form, while the common reciters read it with the doubled zay. Ibn Mas'ud read "ʿalayhim lamublisin" with the omission of "min qablihi". Al-ibласу (despair): being in a state of ill condition together with despair of its ending.

Then He expresses wonder by an address intended for all people, concerning the mercy of Allah, which is the rain. Ibn Kathir, Nafi' and Abu ʿAmr read "athari" in the singular. Ibn ʿAmir, Hamza and al-Kisa'i read "athari" in the plural, and it is differently reported from ʿAsim.

His saying "kayfa yuhyi" may allow that the pronoun in the verb refers to "al-athar" (the trace), and may allow that it refers to Allah, the Exalted, and this is more apparent. A group read "kayfa tahya" with an open taʾ, "al-ardu" in the nominative. Al-Jahdari, Ibn al-Sumayfaʿ and Abu Haywa read "tuhyi" with a damma on the taʾ, on the basis that the verb is attributed to the pronoun of mercy in the accusative. Abu al-Fath said: His saying "kayfa tuhyi" is a sentence in the accusative position as a circumstantial clause (hal), by way of interpretation of meaning, as though He said "muhyiyya" (giving life), and this life and death are a metaphor for drought and the greening of vegetation. Then He, blessed and exalted, informed, by way of analogy and as an alert to it, of resurrection and rising again. His, glorified be He, saying "ʿala kulli shayʾin" is general.

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 30, verses 51–53:

The words of the Most High:

﴿And if We send a wind and they see it turn yellow, they would certainly remain disbelievers after it.﴾ ﴿So indeed you cannot make the dead hear, nor can you make the deaf hear the call when they turn their backs and flee.﴾ ﴿Nor can you guide the blind away from their error. You can only make hear those who believe in Our signs, and they are submitters.﴾

Then the Most High informs of the state of the fluctuation of the son of Adam, in that he is quick to rejoice at rain. When God sends a wind and the vegetation turns yellow because of it, he keeps disbelieving, anxious about it, with little reliance (tawakkul) on God and little submission (taslim) to Him, mighty and majestic is He.

The pronoun in ﴿"fa-ra'awhu"﴾ refers to the vegetation, as we have said, or to the trace, which is the greenness of the vegetation through which the earth was brought to life. Some people said it refers to the cloud, and some said it refers to the wind, but all of this is weak. The lam in "la-in" announces the coming of an oath, and in ﴿"la-zallu"﴾ the lam is the lam of the oath. The words of the Most High "zallu" are a past-tense verb that is treated as if it were in the future and substituted for it, because the conditional response here can only be a future verb; yet the past tense is used in place of the future in some contexts to confirm that the event will certainly occur.

The words of the Most High ﴿"So indeed you cannot make the dead hear"﴾ and the verse... are a metaphor for the disbelievers. The discussion of a similar verse has already been given in Surah al-Naml. All of them read "lā tusmiʿu" with a damma on the taʾ and the accusative "al-ṣumma" (naṣb). Ibn Kathir and ʿAbbas, on the authority of Abu ʿAmr, read "tasmaʿu" with a fatha on the yaʾ and the nominative "al-ṣummu" (rafʿ). The majority read ﴿"bi-hādi al-ʿumy"﴾ with the genitive construction (iḍāfa), while Yahya ibn al-Harith and Abu Haywa read "bi-hādin" with tanwin and "al-ʿumya" in the accusative. The words ﴿"in tusmiʿu illā man yuʾminu"﴾ mean: if you make hear a hearing that benefits and is useful; as for the hearing of the disbelievers, it is not useful, so the two are equal. The words of the Most High ﴿"ʿan ḍalālatihim"﴾: since guidance implies turning away, it is construed with "ʿan" just as "ṣarf" is construed with it. The meaning of the verse is: it is not within your power, O Muhammad, nor is it your duty, to guide. Ibn Abi ʿAbla read "min ḍalālatihim."

﴿It is Allah who created you from weakness, then made after weakness strength, then made after strength weakness and gray hair.
